title: Dimension-preserving search-to-decision reductions for SVP
formal: Does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time oracle reduction that, using only \(\gamma\)-GapSVP queries on lattices of the same dimension \(n\), solves SVP with approximation factor polynomial in \(n\) and \(\gamma\)? Concretely, do there exist absolute positive integers \(C,a,b\) and one randomized oracle machine \(R\) such that for every \(n\ge1\), every nonsingular \(B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), every rational \(\gamma\ge1\), and every admissible oracle \(O_\gamma\) below, \(R^{O_\gamma}(B,\gamma)\) runs in at most \(C(N+2)^b\) steps and outputs \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}\) with \[ \Pr\!\left[\|Bz\|_2\le C(n\gamma)^a\lambda_1(L(B))\right]\ge2/3? \] Here \(N\) is the bit length of the encoded input, and the probability is over the reduction’s random bits.
why: Search returns a short lattice vector, whereas a decision oracle only certifies which side of a length gap the lattice lies on. Bridging these versions with polynomial approximation loss and no dimension increase would sharpen a basic computational relationship at the center of lattice algorithms and worst-case hardness assumptions in cryptography.
status_note: The target is explicitly open in Bennett’s 24 January 2023 source. The near-exact 2016 theorem and the older reduction-map convention were checked directly, as were the dated June 2022 workshop questions. Bounded later searches through 14 September 2026 located no verified matching same-dimension classical reduction with polynomial loss. Recent LWE/LPN search-to-decision results concern different average-case problems and were not treated as resolutions. This is a limited source review, not exhaustive current-status or Lean proof certification.

progress.text: Dimension-preserving randomized reductions are proved for near-exact approximation factors with a substantially larger loss outside that regime.
The Simons Lattices Program lists related approximate search-to-decision questions for CVP and SIVP, with separate classical and quantum conventions.
Open Problem 4.5 explicitly asks for same-dimension SVP-to-GapSVP reduction with search approximation factor \(\operatorname{poly}(\gamma,n)\).

sentences: The input is a rational lattice basis, and the search task is to produce a nonzero vector whose length approximates the shortest possible length.
The available oracle only distinguishes short-vector lengths across a multiplicative gap.
The question asks for a classical polynomial-time reduction that keeps every query in the original dimension and loses only a polynomial in dimension and approximation factor.
Known exact and near-exact reductions do not supply this guarantee across the full approximation range.
A resolution would clarify whether approximate lattice decision algorithms can be converted efficiently into search algorithms without an exponential dimensional penalty.

definitions:
The input lattice is \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), with a rational full-rank square basis whose columns generate it. The Euclidean norm is \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_i x_i^2)^{1/2}\), and \(\lambda_1(L)=\min\{\|v\|_2:v\in L,\ v\ne0\}\). The output is an exact integer coefficient vector \(z\), so its nonzero lattice vector is unambiguously represented even when coordinates are rational. There is no norm other than \(\ell_2\), target point, uniqueness promise, preprocessing of a fixed lattice, or ideal-lattice restriction.

An oracle query is \((\widetilde B,r)\), where \(\widetilde B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular and \(r\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\). An admissible \(O_\gamma\) is any total Boolean function on these valid queries satisfying \[ \lambda_1(L(\widetilde B))\le r\implies O_\gamma(\widetilde B,r)=1,\qquad \lambda_1(L(\widetilde B))>\gamma r\implies O_\gamma(\widetilde B,r)=0.\] When \(r<\lambda_1(L(\widetilde B))\le\gamma r\), its answer can be either bit. The reduction must succeed for every such total completion of the promise problem, including completions with no computability assumption. Repeated identical queries have the same answer because the oracle is a function. The same input value \(\gamma\) applies to every query. At \(\gamma=1\) there is no gap.

Dimension preservation means every oracle lattice has exactly the original dimension \(n\), including its ambient dimension and rank. Queries may use different bases and thresholds, but cannot increase dimension even by an additive constant. This follows the explicit same-\(n\) statement of Open Problem 4.5. Adaptively chosen queries are allowed; this is a Cook (oracle Turing) reduction, not a requirement of one nonadaptive query.

Integers, rational numerators and positive denominators are encoded in binary with signs and delimiters; \(N\) includes the entire basis and \(\gamma\). Use a probabilistic multitape oracle Turing machine with independent unbiased coin flips, a read-only input tape, work tapes and a query tape. Writing a query and reading its one-bit answer are charged; the oracle itself returns that bit in one oracle step. All arithmetic is implemented on binary tapes and pays its full bit cost. The displayed polynomial bounds total time on every random tape and every admissible oracle, and therefore bounds the number and bit lengths of queries and output. Only valid full-rank rational queries are allowed. There is no additional oracle, advice, quantum computation, or free real arithmetic.

The constants and the finite program are fixed before \(n,B,\gamma\) and the oracle are chosen. A bound \(C(n\gamma)^a\) expresses an unspecified polynomial loss uniformly over the domain \(n,\gamma\ge1\); replacing it by any fixed polynomial in these two parameters gives the same polynomial-loss existence target after increasing \(C,a\). The chosen reduction is allowed bounded-error randomness. This makes explicit the classical randomized reduction convention used by the cited near-exact results, rather than adding a deterministic-only requirement.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a reduction and uniform polynomial bounds exist, with correctness against every admissible completion of the promise oracle, or prove their nonexistence. A positive result must bound the output norm, bit complexity, and dimension of every query. Preserving dimension only up to an unbounded factor, obtaining an approximation loss exponential in \(n\), assuming special lattices, or giving only a quantum reduction does not meet the target. The known exact case or approximation factors approaching one alone do not establish the quantified statement.

context_blocks.text: The source asks for polynomial loss in the approximation factor, not exact preservation of that factor. It also explicitly retains dimension. This matters for lattice algorithms whose costs depend exponentially on dimension, and for distinguishing an algorithm that recognizes short vectors from one that actually finds them.

The search and decision versions are known to be equivalent under dimension-preserving reductions in the exact case \(\gamma=1\). The 2016 randomized reduction has search loss \(\gamma^{n/s}\) and running time \(2^{O(s)}\gamma^{O(n)}\), for \(s\ge\log(n+1)\), with input-bit polynomial factors suppressed in that summary. Choosing \(s\) logarithmic gives an efficient useful guarantee when \(\gamma\) is very close to one; it does not give a polynomial-loss polynomial-time reduction for all approximation factors.

Bennett’s 2023 problem is phrased using rational square bases and Euclidean length. The older reduction map uses a relaxed convention that permits an additive constant in dimension, while the card follows the later explicit same-dimension wording. The distinction is recorded so that a looser reduction is not silently counted as satisfying the target.

The source relates a solution at polynomial approximation factors to worst-case search-SVP foundations for lattice cryptography. The Simons list also discusses search-to-decision questions for closest vectors and independent short vectors, including quantum variants. Those questions have different outputs, oracles or computational models and do not settle the reduction here.
